intro.text: **Built for live conversations.** Pick who you're talking to, then go to **🗡️ Offense** (you bring the case) or **🛡️ Defense** (they raised an objection).
Doctrinal frame: our church's Articles of Faith. One Being, three Persons; Christ has two natures; Scripture alone.

Pray first. Only the Spirit opens eyes (John 6:44; 2 Cor 4:4–6). Watch your own heart for pride; the goal is their soul, not the point (2 Tim 2:24–26). What helps in real conversations isn't knowing more verses. It's **how you run the conversation**. Use these moves every time.

moves.title: Phase 1 = agree on the plain text. Nothing else moves until they do.
moves.text: Read the verse and ask a yes/no question about what it *says* (not what it means). Don't go on until they answer. *"I'm not moving to Phase 2 until you answer Phase 1."*

moves.title: Yes/no questions, one at a time.
moves.text: *"Does the Holy Spirit speak? Yes or no?"* Short questions are hard to wriggle out of. Long statements give them room to filibuster.

moves.title: Call out the dodge out loud.
moves.text: When they redefine a word ("personification," "communicates information," "a vibe"), name it: *"I didn't ask about personification. I asked, can He speak?"*

moves.title: Use their rule on another verse.
moves.text: When they invent a rule for one verse (e.g. "no article = 'a god'"), apply the same rule somewhere it obviously fails (John 1:6 becomes "a man sent from *a god* named *a John*").

moves.title: Hold them to their own analogy.
moves.text: If they bring an analogy (king and messenger, software coder, three judges), don't swap it out. Push it until it proves your point: *"Can the agent of the king claim to BE the king?"*

moves.title: No topic-hopping.
moves.text: When a point lands, people often jump to "Is Jesus God?" or "the Trinity makes no sense." Don't follow. *"Let's finish this one first, then I'm happy to go there."*

moves.title: Name the goalpost shift.
moves.text: *"First you wanted a Bible verse. I gave you the verse. Now it has to come from Jesus' own mouth?"*

moves.title: "What's the only thing we do? Read."
moves.text: When they say "context," make *them* show the verse in the context. Then wait. Silence works for you.

moves.title: Ask the question back.
moves.text: End with a question they have to answer on their own (*"Who is the Father hearing from?"*), not a speech.

moves.title: Stay warm.
moves.text: Even when they get angry or walk away: *"I want you to be saved, brother. I love you."* Truth with love keeps the door open (1 Pet 3:15–16).

universalTools.title: "Yahweh" isn't one-person-only.
universalTools.text: Yahweh is the name of the one true God, and Scripture applies it to the Father, the Son and the Spirit. Their "then Jesus is his own Father" syllogism only works if Yahweh = the Father alone. A name can have more than one referent: "Judah" can mean a man *or* a tribe (Judges 1:1–2).

universalTools.title: Word–concept fallacy.
universalTools.text: "'Trinity' isn't in the Bible" → neither are "monotheism" or "Bible." The question is whether the *concept* is there.

universalTools.title: Three in one way, one in another.
universalTools.text: Not a contradiction. Different categories: 3 *persons*, 1 *being*. (With a Muslim: the Quran comes in several transmitted readings, such as Hafs, Warsh and Qalun, and Muslims still say it is one Quran.)

universalTools.title: Context decides literal vs. figurative.
universalTools.text: Both sides agree personification exists. But personified things don't say "set apart for **me**" or "the work **I** have called them to."

universalTools.title: "Firstborn" = rank, not birth order.
universalTools.text: David was the *youngest* son and the *second* king, yet God calls him "firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth" (Ps 89:27).

holySpiritPlay.title: 🔥 THE HOLY SPIRIT PLAY: "the Spirit is Yahweh" (Unitarians, JWs, Oneness, Muslims)

intro.text: **Why this works:** Unitarians spend all their energy on Jesus (agency, *shaliach*, "a god"). They usually have **no prepared answer for the Spirit**. Two steps: **(A) the Spirit is a Person → (B) that Person is Yahweh.**

stepA.title: Step A: The Spirit is a *Who*, not a *what*

opener.text: *"Does the Holy Spirit speak? Yes or no?"*

rows.point: "Set apart for **me** Barnabas and Saul for the work to which **I** have called them." First-person speech, a choice, authority.
rows.question: *"Do actions have authority, or do persons?"* / *"He said 'I' and 'me' about Himself. That's self-awareness, right?"*

rows.point: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit **and to us**." He takes part in a decision alongside the apostles.
rows.question: *"Can a force agree with a council?"*

rows.point: He can be grieved and rebelled against.
rows.question: *"An active force can't be offended. Whoever the Spirit is, He's someone you **can** offend."*

rows.point: He "does not speak on His own; whatever He **hears** He speaks."
rows.question: (vs. Oneness or "Spirit = the Father") *"Who is the Father hearing from?"*
*"Christ is called God's power and He's a person. So being God's power doesn't rule out being a person, right?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"That's personification."*
ifTheySay.youSay: *"I didn't ask about figurative language. Can He speak, yes or no? If I say 'my car told me it's not starting today,' did my car speak?"*. Then: personified wisdom never chooses missionaries in real time (Acts 13:2).

ifTheySay.theySay: *"He just communicates information / He has no mouth."*
ifTheySay.youSay: *"Does the Father have a mouth? Does the Father speak?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"The Father told the Spirit to say it."*
ifTheySay.youSay: The text says "for **me**… **I** have called." That's not quoting someone else.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"He's rational energy, like AI."*
ifTheySay.youSay: AI is programmed. The Spirit wills, commands and is provoked. *"Can energy be rational without personhood?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"God used the Spirit's power to create."*
ifTheySay.youSay: God also created *through Christ* (John 1:3), and Christ is a person.

stepB.title: Step B: That Person is Yahweh

structure.text: an OT text says **Yahweh** spoke → the NT says **the Holy Spirit** said it.

rows.second: **Acts 4:24–25**: the "Sovereign Lord… who **by the Holy Spirit**, through the mouth of David"
rows.note: Go-to question: *"So the Sovereign Lord who spoke through David is who?"*

rows.second: **Heb 3:7–11**: "As **the Holy Spirit says**… they tested **Me**… I swore in **My** wrath"
rows.note: *"Who is the Spirit talking about when He says 'they provoked **Me**'?"*

rows.second: **Acts 28:25–26**: "**The Holy Spirit** was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah, 'Go to this people…'"
rows.note: Also John 12:41: Isaiah saw *Christ's* glory. One vision, three Persons.

rows.second: **Heb 10:15–17**: "**The Holy Spirit** also bears witness… 'This is the covenant **I** will make'"
rows.note: The Spirit speaks Yahweh's covenant in the first person.

offense.title: Only God can pay the ransom
offense.subtitle: Psalm 49

chain.text: **Ps 49:7–9**: no man can redeem his brother or give God a ransom for him. The redemption price for a soul is costly. *"How many men does the psalm say can pay it?"*
**Ps 49:15**: "But **God** will redeem my soul from the power of Sheol." *"So who does the psalmist say will do the redeeming?"*
**Isa 43:11**: Jehovah says, "there is no savior besides Me."
**Mark 10:45; 1 Tim 2:5–6**: Jesus came to give His life as a **ransom** for many. The one mediator gave Himself as a ransom for all.
**Titus 2:13–14**: our great **God and Savior**, Jesus Christ, gave Himself for us that He might **redeem** us.

**John 1:1; John 1:14; Heb 2:14–17**: the Word was God and became flesh. He **partook** of flesh and blood so that through death He might free those enslaved by the fear of death. He had to be man to die in our place, and God to redeem.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Psalm 49 is about imperfect men. Jesus was a perfect man, a corresponding ransom for Adam."*
ifTheySay.youSay: The psalm makes no exception for a perfect man. Its answer is "God will redeem." And every creature worships the Lamb for the people He purchased (Rev 5:9; Rev 5:13–14). *"Would Jehovah share that worship with a creature?"* (Isa 42:8)

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Jehovah provided the ransom. Jesus was only the price."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Yes, the Father sent the Son. But the One who gave Himself is called our great God and Savior (Titus 2:13–14).

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Acts 20:28 should read 'the blood of His own Son.'"*
ifTheySay.youSay: That verse speaks of God purchasing the church with blood. Some manuscripts read "church of the Lord," and some translations say "the blood of His own." Don't rest the case on this one verse; the chain above stands without it.

opener.text: *"According to Psalm 49:7, can any man redeem his brother or give God a ransom for him?"* (They'll say no.)

summary.text: This is a cumulative case. Psalm 49 does not name Jesus, and it does not prove the Trinity on its own. It says no mere man can pay the ransom and that God will redeem. The New Testament then says Jesus paid it, and calls Him God.

closer.text: *"If no man can pay the ransom, and God says He will redeem, who is the Jesus who paid it?"*

defense.objection: "John 1:1 says 'a god.' No article = indefinite."
defense.response: A predicate noun before the verb without the article describes **nature** (Harner: qualitative). "The Word was God" in nature: all that God is, the Word was.
defense.goTo: John 1:1; **1 John 4:8** (*ho theos agapē estin*); **John 1:6** (*para theou*, no article)
defense.askBack: *"Is God 'a love'? Was John sent from 'a god'? Your NWT says 'God' in 1:6. Why not in 1:1?"*

defense.objection: "*Ton theon* = the Almighty; *theos* = a lesser god."
defense.response: That's just Greek case. *Ton theon* is accusative after *pros*; *theos* is nominative. Case endings aren't ranks.
defense.askBack: *"Is the Father a lesser god when he's in the nominative?"*

defense.objection: "Firstborn of creation" (Col 1:15) = first created
defense.response: *Prōtotokos* = preeminent heir. v.16 gives the reason: "**because** by Him all things were created."
defense.askBack: *"Who was Israel's first king? Saul. So how is David 'firstborn' of the kings?"*

defense.objection: "Only-begotten" (John 3:16) = uniquely created
defense.response: *Monogenēs* = the unique, only begotten Son, never "created" (Heb 11:17: Isaac wasn't Abraham's only son).
defense.askBack: *"Was Isaac Abraham's only child?"*

defense.objection: "Beginning of the creation of God" (Rev 3:14)
defense.response: *Archē* = origin / ruler / source. He's where creation comes from.
defense.askBack: *"If you're the originator of your business, aren't you its origin?"*

defense.objection: "John 5:19: Jesus can do nothing on his own"
defense.response: That shows the Persons are distinct and act together. Finish the verse: "whatever the Father does, **the Son does likewise**."
defense.askBack: *"Does the Father do anything without the Son?"*

defense.objection: "John 14:28: 'the Father is greater than I'"
defense.response: Greater in role, in the Son's humbled human state. Not in nature. Phil 2:6–7.
defense.askBack: *"Is a husband 'greater' in nature than his wife because he leads?"*

defense.objection: "Psalm 8 / Heb 2: everything is subject to *man*, not Jesus"
defense.response: Heb 2:9 identifies the "him": "**namely Jesus**."
defense.askBack: *"Who are we going to trust, you or the author of Hebrews?"*

defense.objection: "Daniel 7: Jesus wasn't seated / Rev 3:21: believers sit on the throne too"
defense.response: Sharing kingdom authority ≠ sitting **on high** in heaven, the place that belongs to Yahweh alone (Ps 113:5).
defense.askBack: *"Show me anyone other than Jesus who sits 'on high' at the right hand of the Majesty."*

defense.objection: "Holy Spirit = active force"
defense.response: → [🔥 Holy Spirit Play](#holy-spirit-play)
defense.askBack: *"Can a force be grieved?"*

defense.objection: "Trinity isn't in the Bible."
defense.response: Word–concept fallacy. "Jehovah's Witness" isn't in the Bible as a denomination name either. Is the *concept* taught?
defense.askBack: *"Is the word 'theocracy' in the Bible?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus is Michael the Archangel."
defense.response: Scripture never says it. Michael did not dare rebuke Satan himself (Jude 9); Jesus commands him directly (Matt 4:10). God never called any angel "My Son," and **all** the angels worship the Son.
defense.askBack: *"To which of the angels did God ever say, 'You are My Son'?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus was raised as a spirit, not in a body."
defense.response: He said a spirit does not have flesh and bones as He has, He showed His wounds, and He said He would raise **His body**.
defense.askBack: *"In John 2:19–21, what did Jesus say He would raise?"*

defense.objection: "Only 144,000 go to heaven."
defense.response: Right after the 144,000, John sees a great multitude **no one could count** standing before the throne, serving God in His temple.
defense.askBack: *"Where is the great multitude standing in Rev 7:9?"*

defense.objection: "The dead are unconscious. The soul stops existing."
defense.response: Paul expected to depart and **be with Christ**, away from the body and at home with the Lord. The souls under the altar speak.
defense.askBack: *"How do the souls in Rev 6:10 cry out if they don't exist?"*

defense.objection: "Hell isn't eternal. The wicked are simply destroyed."
defense.response: Jesus uses the same word, "eternal," for the punishment and for the life in one sentence.
defense.askBack: *"If the punishment isn't eternal, is the life?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus died on a stake, not a cross."
defense.response: Don't make this the fight. Thomas speaks of **nails**, plural, in His hands, and the sign was placed above His **head**. Then go back to who Jesus is.
defense.askBack: *"Why 'nails,' plural, for His hands?"*

defense.objection: "You must use God's name, Jehovah."
defense.response: The apostles take the Old Testament "name" texts and apply them to **Jesus**. Joel's "call on the name of Yahweh" becomes confessing Jesus as Lord.
defense.askBack: *"In Rom 10:13, whose name is in view, given verse 9?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus is a god, a mighty one, but not the true God."
defense.response: Jehovah says no god was formed before or after Him and He knows of no other. So is Jesus a true God or a false god? Thomas calls Him "my Lord and **my God**" and Jesus accepts it.
defense.askBack: *"Is Jesus a true god or a false god?"*

defense.objection: "People only did obeisance to Jesus, not worship."
defense.response: All the angels worship the Son. Every creature gives the same honor to God and to the Lamb. An angel refuses it; Jesus receives it.
defense.askBack: *"Why does the angel refuse what Jesus accepts?"*

defense.objection: "You need Jehovah's organization to be saved."
defense.response: Salvation is by grace through faith, not works, and not membership. When others left, Peter did not ask **where** to go, but **to whom**.
defense.askBack: *"To whom did Peter say we should go?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus was a perfect man, a corresponding ransom for Adam. He didn't need to be God."
defense.response: He had to be truly man to die in our place. But Scripture says no man can ransom another, and that God Himself redeems. The One who paid is the Word, who was God and became flesh. Run [Only God can pay the ransom](/jw/case/play-6).
defense.askBack: *"Psalm 49 says no man can pay it. So what kind of man is Jesus?"*

offense.title: The Angel of Yahweh claims to be God, with no "thus says the Lord"

chain.text: **Gen 31:11–13**: "the **Angel of God** said… '**I am the God of Bethel**, where you anointed a pillar and made a vow **to me**.'"

ifTheySay.theySay: *"*Malak* means a lesser being, sent by a superior."*

opener.text: *"You say Islam is morally superior. Can we read a few verses of the Quran and see?"*

defense.objection: "How can God be 3 and 1?"
defense.response: Three in one sense (**Persons**), one in another (**Being**). Different categories, no contradiction.
defense.askBack: *"The Quran has several transmitted readings: Hafs, Warsh, Qalun. Is that three Qurans, or one?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus never said 'I am God, worship me.'"
defense.response: He said things only God could say, and accepted what only God receives. Watch for the goalpost shift.
defense.askBack: *"First you wanted a verse. Now it has to come from Jesus' mouth?"*

defense.objection: "God is not a man" (Hosea 11:9)
defense.response: Correct by nature. The Son **added** a human nature. Two natures, one Person. And don't let them skip the verse you gave first.
defense.askBack: *"Do you acknowledge Heb 1:3 says the Son is the exact imprint of God's nature?"*

defense.objection: "Which God sent Jesus? Who was He praying to?"
defense.response: One God, three Persons. The **Father** sent the **Son**. Jesus prayed as a true man.
defense.askBack: *"In John 17:5 Jesus asks for the glory He had with the Father before the world existed. Can a mere prophet pray that?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus wasn't crucified" (Q 4:157)
defense.response: Every early source, Christian and non-Christian (Josephus c. AD 93, Tacitus c. AD 116), agrees He was crucified. The Quran denies it 600 years later with no source. And the Injil the Quran confirms teaches it.
defense.askBack: *"Who did Allah make look like Jesus, and did he deceive the disciples into starting Christianity?"*

defense.objection: "Paul corrupted Jesus' message."
defense.response: Paul's gospel was checked and approved by Peter, James and John. And Q 61:14 praises Jesus' disciples as Allah's helpers, who won.
defense.askBack: *"Q 61:14 says Allah made Jesus' followers victorious. The faith that won taught what Paul taught. Did Allah back the wrong side?"*

defense.objection: "The Torah is one book, but you have five."
defense.response: The Torah = Genesis to Deuteronomy, the five books of Moses: one Torah in five scrolls. Jewish tradition says Joshua added the account of Moses' death (Deut 34).
defense.askBack: *"The Quran has 114 surahs. Is it 114 books, or one?"*

defense.objection: "The Trinity is pagan / Allah is 'the third of three'"
defense.response: The Quran pictures worship of God, Jesus and **Mary** (Q 5:116; cf. Q 5:73–75). That is not the Trinity Christians believe: one God in three Persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
defense.askBack: *"Which Christian ever taught Mary is part of the Trinity?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus ate, slept and prayed. God doesn't do that."
defense.response: He is truly God and truly man. The Word **became flesh**. Hunger and sleep belong to His human nature; they don't cancel His divine nature.
defense.askBack: *"If God chose to enter His creation as a man, who could stop Him?"*

defense.objection: "The Injil was one book given to Jesus. You have four, written by men."
defense.response: "Gospel" means the good news about Jesus. And the Quran tells the people of the Gospel to judge by what they **had** in the 7th century, which was these four.
defense.askBack: *"What Gospel did Christians have in Muhammad's day?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel."
defense.response: His earthly ministry went to Israel first, as promised. Then He sent His disciples to **all nations**, as Isaiah foretold.
defense.askBack: *"Who does Jesus send them to in Matt 28:19?"*

defense.objection: "The Bible has contradictions and too many versions."
defense.response: Translations are not different Bibles. The manuscript differences are known and printed in the footnotes, and no teaching depends on them. Ask for one and read it together.
defense.askBack: *"Which contradiction? Let's read it."*

defense.objection: "God can simply forgive. He doesn't need a sacrifice."
defense.response: A judge who lets the guilty go is unjust. God will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. At the cross He is both **just and the justifier**. Even the Quran ransoms Abraham's son with a great sacrifice.
defense.askBack: *"If a judge lets the guilty go free, is he a just judge?"*

defense.objection: "No one can carry another person's sins (Q 6:164)."
defense.response: The Torah the Quran confirms is built on substitution: the sins of the people laid on another. Isaiah foretold One who would bear the iniquity of us all. And Jesus is not an unwilling bystander punished for a stranger. He is the Son who laid down His life of His own accord, as the Father purposed.
defense.askBack: *"What does Isaiah 53:6 say Yahweh laid on Him?"*

defense.objection: "Your own Bible says each person dies for his own sin (Deut 24:16; Ezek 18:20)."
defense.response: Deuteronomy tells human courts not to execute a son for his father's crime. Ezekiel says God holds each person to account for his own sin. Both forbid punishing an unwilling innocent. Neither forbids a willing substitute whom God Himself appoints. The same Law commands the sacrifices, and Isaiah foretells the Servant who bears the sin of many.
defense.askBack: *"If substitution is forbidden, what are the sacrifices in Leviticus for?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus was only a prophet. A prophet can't redeem anyone."
defense.response: Agreed: no mere man can. The Psalms say no man can ransom his brother, and that God Himself will redeem. That is why the Redeemer had to be God become man. Jesus said He came to give His life as a ransom.
defense.askBack: *"If no man can pay the ransom, who can?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus and His disciples were Muslims."
defense.response: His disciples worshiped Him, called Him Lord and God, and preached that He was crucified and raised.
defense.askBack: *"Would a Muslim say 'My Lord and my God' to Jesus?"*

defense.objection: "Muhammad is named in Song of Songs 5:16."
defense.response: The Hebrew word there is an ordinary word for "desirable," used by a bride about her beloved. The same word family describes Ezekiel's wife (Ezek 24:16) and Israel's children (Hos 9:16).
defense.askBack: *"Is Muhammad also in Ezekiel 24:16, where the same word is used?"*

defense.objection: "Islam is the fastest-growing religion, so it must be true."
defense.response: Truth isn't a headcount. Jesus said the many take the wide road.
defense.askBack: *"Is something true because many people believe it?"*

defense.objection: "The Quran is a miracle. No one can produce a chapter like it."
defense.response: That test has no judge and no standard. The Quran gives a better test: check with those who read the Scripture before.
defense.askBack: *"Who judges the contest, and by what standard?"*

defense.objection: "Jesus said, 'Why do you call Me good? Only God is good.'"
defense.response: He didn't say He isn't good. He asked the man **why** he said it. Jesus calls Himself the Good Shepherd.
defense.askBack: *"Is Jesus good?"*

beliefs.text: Revelation reaches us through Scripture *and* Sacred Tradition, and "both… must be accepted and honoured with equal sentiments of devotion and reverence" [CCC 82; Trent, Sess. 4]. Only the Magisterium (the pope and the bishops in communion with him) can interpret either one authentically [CCC 85, 100]. Justification "is conferred in Baptism" and "makes us inwardly just" [CCC 1992]. No one can merit the first grace, but the justified "can then merit for ourselves and for others… the attainment of eternal life" [CCC 2010]. The Mass is "one single sacrifice" with the cross, offered "in reparation for the sins of the living and the dead" [CCC 1367, 1414]. Mortal sin destroys sanctifying grace, and it is restored through confession to a priest [CCC 1446, 1456, 1861]. Those who die "imperfectly purified" undergo purgatory before heaven [CCC 1030–1031].

lead.label: Where we agree
lead.text: They confess one God in three Persons, the full deity and humanity of Christ, the virgin birth, the bodily resurrection, the return of Christ, and eternal judgment [CCC 1035, 1040]. They affirm that Scripture is inspired, and that "no one can merit the initial grace" [CCC 2010]. Say this plainly. The disagreement is not over *whether* Jesus is God; it is over *how a sinner is made right with Him*, and over *who has the final word*.

lead.label: Approach
lead.text: Most Catholics you'll talk to are family and friends who have never read the Catechism or Trent. Many are sincere and devout, and they are trusting a system that cannot save. Be gentle with the person and give no ground on the gospel. For the strongest statement of the case, see [MacArthur on Rome](/topic/macarthur-on-rome). The goal is "not just to win arguments, but more importantly to win souls". Two things keep it clear. First, they use the same words with a different meaning: "grace," "faith," and "justification" all mean something different in Rome. Define terms before you argue. Second, keep coming back to two questions: *What is your final authority?* and *Is Christ's work enough by itself?*.

cheatCard.text: **Rom 4:4–5**: *"Does God justify the one who works, or the one who believes?"*
**Heb 10:14, 18**: *"If His one offering perfected us for all time, and there's no longer any offering for sin, what is offered at Mass?"*
**1 Tim 2:5**: *"How many mediators between God and men does Paul name?"*
**Mark 7:8–13**: *"Can a religious tradition ever cancel out God's word?"*
**1 John 5:13**: *"John wrote so you can *know* you have eternal life. Do you?"*
**Gal 1:8–9**: *"If even an apostle or an angel can't change the gospel, can a council?"*

altOpeners.text: *"What do you think makes a person right with God: what Christ did, what we do, or both?"*

*"If God asked you, 'Why should I let you into My heaven?', what would you say?"* (Listen for "I" answers: I tried, I went to Mass, I was baptized. The only answer that stands is Christ and His righteousness.)

chain.text: **Rom 3:23–24**: All have sinned, and are justified as a *gift*, by His grace. *"Is a gift paid for in any part?"*
**Rom 3:28**: Justified by faith *apart from* works of the Law. *"What does 'apart from' leave out?"*
**Rom 4:4–5**: To the worker, wages are owed. To "the one who does not work, but believes," faith is credited as righteousness. *"Which one is Abraham?"*
**Rom 4:6–8**: David speaks of righteousness credited "apart from works." *"Is that righteousness *in* David, or credited *to* David?"*
**2 Cor 5:21; Phil 3:9**: Our sin was credited to Christ, and His righteousness to us, "not… my own… but… through faith." *"Whose righteousness do you want to stand in on Judgment Day?"*
**Rom 5:1**: "Having been justified by faith, we have peace." *"Is that peace now, or only after purgatory?"*

**Rom 6:23; Luke 18:9–14**: Death is a *wage*. Eternal life is a *free gift*. The tax collector brought no record, only a plea for mercy, and he went home justified. *"Can the same thing be both a wage you earn and a gift you're given?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"'Works of the law' means only the Jewish ceremonies."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Rom 4:4–5 talks about *any* work that earns wages. Eph 2:8–9 says "not of works," and Titus 3:5 says not by "deeds which we have done in righteousness." *"Are deeds done in righteousness ceremonies?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"We believe in grace too. The Catechism says no one can merit the first grace."*
ifTheySay.youSay: They will quote [CCC 2010]. Read the rest of it. The same paragraph says the justified then *merit* "the attainment of eternal life." Rom 11:6 says grace and works can't be mixed: "otherwise grace is no longer grace."

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Trent only condemns a dead faith, with no cooperation."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Read the canon they mean. Trent condemns anyone who says justification is "by faith alone… [so] that nothing else is required to co-operate" [Trent, Sess. 6, can. 9]. It also condemns justification by "the sole imputation of the justice of Christ" [can. 11]. That is exactly Rom 4:5. Sproul: if the Reformers were right, Trent anathematized the gospel.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Faith alone means you can live however you want."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Saving faith comes with repentance and produces works (Eph 2:10; Titus 2:11–14; Rom 6:1–4). Works are the *fruit* of justification, not its *cause*. Trent condemns that very sentence [Sess. 6, can. 24].

ifTheySay.theySay: *"That sounds too easy."*
ifTheySay.youSay: It cost Christ everything; it costs us our pride. Paul had the best religious record of anyone, and he counted all of it as loss so that he could be found in Christ with a righteousness that was not his own (Phil 3:4–9). The jailer asked what he must do, and the answer was "Believe in the Lord Jesus" (Acts 16:30–31). *"What would you have to give up to come to God with empty hands?"*

opener.text: *"Do you know for sure that if you died today you'd be with God?"* (Most will say "I hope so" or "No one can know." The rest of the play explains why the answer can be yes.)

closer.text: *"God's offer is Christ's righteousness credited to you the moment you turn from sin and trust Him alone (Mark 1:15; Rom 4:5). Not Christ plus your record. Would you trust Him that way today?"*

altOpeners.text: *"Is the sacrifice of the Mass a real sacrifice for sins?"* (A Catholic who knows the faith will say yes [Trent, Sess. 22, can. 1, 3].)

chain.text: **Heb 7:27**: Unlike the priests, He offered Himself "once for all." *"How many times?"*
**Heb 9:25–28**: Not "often," or He would have to suffer often. He was "offered once to bear the sins of many." *"Can a sacrifice for sin be offered without suffering, according to v. 26?"*
**Heb 10:11–12**: The priests "stand daily" offering sacrifices that never take away sins. Christ offered one sacrifice and "sat down." *"Why does the writer contrast standing with sitting?"*
**Heb 10:14**: By one offering He "has perfected for all time" those who are sanctified. *"What's left for a priest to add?"*
**Heb 10:18**: "Where there is forgiveness of these things, there is no longer any offering for sin." *"So what is offered on the altar each Sunday?"*

**Heb 9:11–12; Rom 6:9–10**: He entered the holy place once, "having obtained eternal redemption," and He is "never to die again." Rome says that at each Mass "the work of our redemption is carried out" [CCC 1364]. *"Is redemption obtained, or still being carried out?"*

**1 Cor 11:26; Luke 22:19**: The Supper *proclaims* His death "until He comes" and is done "in remembrance." *"Is a proclamation the same thing as an offering?"* At the table Jesus said, "given for you." *"In the upper room, who is giving to whom?"*

chain.label: Why it matters
chain.text: The English Reformers were burned chiefly over this doctrine. It isn't a side issue.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"It's not a new sacrifice. It's the same sacrifice made present."*
ifTheySay.youSay: That is what Rome says [CCC 1366–1367]. Trent still calls the Mass "propitiatory," "offered for the living and the dead, for sins" [Sess. 22, can. 3], and the Catechism says it is "offered in reparation for the sins of the living and the dead" [CCC 1414]. Heb 10:18 says that where forgiveness exists, *no* offering for sin remains. *"If sins still need an offering, were they forgiven at the cross?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Malachi 1:11 predicts a pure offering among the nations."*
ifTheySay.youSay: In context it is the worship of God's name spreading among the Gentiles. The NT calls praise (Heb 13:15) and our bodies (Rom 12:1) sacrifices. It never calls the Supper a sacrifice for sin. (Inference from the NT pattern. The NT does not quote Mal 1:11.)

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Jesus said 'This is My body.'"*
ifTheySay.youSay: He also said "I am the door" (John 10:9). He said it while His body stood in front of them, holding the bread. Our church holds that the elements are representative, *and* that the Supper is a real communion with the risen Christ (1 Cor 10:16). See the John 6 row in the defense table.

opener.text: *"When Jesus said 'It is finished' on the cross, what was finished?"* (John 19:30)

closer.text: *"Hebrews is clear that His sacrifice is never repeated. If His one offering is enough, you don't need another one. You need Him. Will you rest on what He finished (Heb 10:14)?"*

altOpeners.text: *"What did Mary herself tell people to do about Jesus?"* (John 2:5: "Whatever He says to you, do it.")

chain.text: **1 Tim 2:5**: "One mediator also between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." *"Did Paul leave room for a second?"*
**Heb 4:14–16**: Because of our High Priest, *we* draw near to the throne "with confidence." *"Do we need someone to approach Jesus for us?"*
**Heb 7:25**: He "always lives to make intercession." *"Is His intercession ever not enough?"*
**Luke 11:27–28**: A woman blesses Mary's womb. Jesus answers, "On the contrary, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it." *"Why did Jesus redirect the praise?"*
**Luke 1:47**: Mary calls God "my Savior." *"Who needs a Savior?"* (Rom 3:23)
**Acts 10:25–26; Rev 22:8–9**: Peter and an angel both refuse religious bowing. "Worship God." *"If an apostle and an angel refused it, should Mary receive it?"*

**Luke 1:38; Matt 12:46–50; Acts 1:14**: Mary calls herself the Lord's slave. Jesus says whoever does His Father's will is His brother and sister and mother. After the ascension she prays *with* the disciples, no one prays *to* her, and she is not named again. *"Where in the New Testament does anyone pray to Mary?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"We don't worship Mary. We give her hyperdulia, not latria."*
ifTheySay.youSay: The distinction is Rome's, not the Bible's. Scripture doesn't grade religious service this way: Paul uses the *dulia* word for serving the living God (1 Thess 1:9) and for the bondage of serving "those which by nature are no gods" (Gal 4:8). Rome does teach it, and Vatican II says her role "neither takes away from nor adds anything to" Christ's [LG 62]. Then ask where Scripture teaches *any* category of religious honor or prayer directed to a creature. Peter and the angel refused even the bowing (Acts 10:25–26; Rev 22:8–9).

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Asking Mary to pray is like asking you to pray."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Scripture commands believers on earth to pray for one another (James 5:16). It never models or commands praying to the departed. It warns against seeking the dead (Deut 18:10–11; Isa 8:19). Catholics would say the saints are alive in Christ, not "the dead," so present this as an inference. Also, a creature who hears millions of silent prayers at once would need a divine attribute.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"The Church calls her Mediatrix [CCC 969], but in a subordinate way."*
ifTheySay.youSay: *"Is 'one mediator' in 1 Tim 2:5 a ranking, or a number?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Rev 5:8 shows saints offering prayers in heaven."*
ifTheySay.youSay: It shows the prayers of God's people presented before Him. It doesn't tell anyone to pray *to* the elders. Ask: *"Who is the prayer addressed to?"*

opener.text: *"When the disciples asked how to pray, who did Jesus tell them to talk to?"* (Matt 6:9: "Our Father.")

closer.text: *"Jesus said, 'Come to Me, all who are weary' (Matt 11:28). Mary pointed to Him too (John 2:5). Will you go straight to Christ, turning from sin and trusting Him alone?"*

offense.title: The rule that tests every rule
offense.subtitle: authority

altOpeners.text: *"If a church teaching and the Bible clearly disagreed, which one would you follow?"*

chain.text: **Mark 7:8–9, 13**: "Neglecting the commandment of God, you hold to the tradition of men… invalidating the word of God." *"Did their tradition claim to come from God?"*
**Matt 22:29, 31**: "You are mistaken, not understanding the Scriptures… have you not read what was spoken to you by God?" *"What did Jesus hold them responsible to know?"*
**Acts 17:11**: The Bereans checked an *apostle* against the Scriptures, and are called noble. *"If Paul could be checked, who can't be?"*
**2 Tim 3:15–17**: Scripture makes us "wise for salvation" and the man of God "fully equipped." *"What's missing from 'fully equipped'?"*
**Gal 1:8–9**: "Even if we, or an angel from heaven" preach another gospel, let him be accursed. *"What does Paul put above even himself?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Who gave you the Bible? The Church!"*
ifTheySay.youSay: See the defense table. God gave it, and His people *received* it. The OT was Scripture before any church existed (Matt 22:31; Rom 3:2).

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Without the Magisterium, your reading is just your private opinion."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Everyone reads, including Catholics who read the Catechism. The question is whether Scripture is clear enough to obey (2 Tim 3:15: Timothy understood it as a child). Vatican II itself says the Magisterium "is not above the word of God, but serves it" [DV 10]. *"Then can Scripture correct it?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"The early church fathers weren't 'Bible-only.'"*
ifTheySay.youSay: Cyril of Jerusalem told his catechumens: "Even to me… do not give absolute credence, unless you receive the proof… from the divine Scriptures".

opener.text: *"Did Jesus ever correct religious leaders who had tradition on their side?"* (Yes: Mark 7.)

closer.text: *"If Scripture is the one rule that can't err, let's let it settle the biggest question: how a sinner is made right with God. Would you read Romans 3–5 with me this week?"*

altOpeners.text: *"Has a priest ever told you that you're definitely going to heaven?"* (Rome says no one has absolute certainty of persevering without a special revelation [Trent, Sess. 6, can. 16; CCC 2005].)

chain.text: **1 John 5:11–13**: "These things I have written… so that you may *know* that you have eternal life." *"Did John say 'hope' or 'know'?"*
**John 5:24**: The one who hears and believes "has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life." *"What tense is 'has'?"*
**John 10:27–29**: "No one will snatch them out of My hand." *"Who's holding whom?"*
**Rom 8:1, 33–34**: "No condemnation." "Who will bring a charge against God's elect? God is the one who justifies." *"If God has declared you righteous, who can overturn it?"*
**Heb 10:14**: "Perfected for all time." *"Then what is purgatory finishing?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Claiming certainty is presumption."*
ifTheySay.youSay: It would be, if it rested on your performance. It rests on Christ's promise (John 6:37–40). Doubting His word is not humility.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Mortal sin can make you lose grace [CCC 1861]."*
ifTheySay.youSay: True faith perseveres because God keeps it (Phil 1:6; 1 Pet 1:5; 1 John 2:19). Our church teaches that the redeemed are kept by God's power forever.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Purgatory isn't hell. It's a purification for the saved [CCC 1030–1031]."*
ifTheySay.youSay: *"Christ 'made purification of sins' (Heb 1:3) and His blood 'cleanses us from all sin' (1 John 1:7). What part of 'all' is left?"* MacArthur: deny justification by faith alone "and you must devise an explanation" for how we reach heaven's perfection.

opener.text: *"Can a person know they have eternal life? Yes or no?"*

closer.text: *"God wants you to know (1 John 5:13). That certainty comes from trusting Christ alone, not from keeping yourself in a state of grace. Will you repent and trust Him today?"*

defense.objection: "The Catholic Church gave you the Bible."
defense.response: God gave it. His people recognized His voice (John 10:27). Jesus held people accountable to the OT before any church existed. The church *received* the canon; it didn't create it.
defense.askBack: *"Who decided the OT canon that Jesus quoted?"*

defense.objection: "Which of the 30,000+ Protestant denominations is right?"
defense.response: The figure comes from an encyclopedia that counted thousands of "denominations" in ways that don't mean doctrinal splits, Catholic ones included. Unity is in the gospel, and Rome has its own deep internal divisions.
defense.askBack: *"Do all Catholics agree on what the Catechism means?"*

defense.objection: "Where was your church before Luther?"
defense.response: Wherever God's people trusted Christ and His word. Busenitz shows justification by grace through faith in the fathers long before 1517, for example Clement of Rome: "not justified by ourselves… but by that faith".
defense.askBack: *"Was the gospel missing before Trent defined it?"*

defense.objection: "James 2:24: 'justified by works and not by faith alone.'"
defense.response: James answers the question *"what kind of faith saves?"* (2:14), and shows a living faith *before people* (2:18: "show me"). Paul answers how a sinner is declared righteous *before God* (Rom 4:2–5). Abraham was credited righteous in Gen 15, decades before Gen 22.
defense.askBack: *"In Gen 15:6, had Abraham offered Isaac yet?"*

defense.objection: "John 6:53: 'Unless you eat My flesh.'"
defense.response: In context, coming = eating and believing = drinking (6:35). He promises eternal life to whoever *believes* (6:40, 47), and He explains: "the flesh profits nothing; the words… are spirit" (6:63). The Supper hadn't been instituted yet.
defense.askBack: *"Does 6:54 promise eternal life to everyone who takes Communion?"*

defense.objection: "John 20:23: priests can forgive sins."
defense.response: Jesus sends the disciples to proclaim forgiveness, which is granted to all who repent and believe (Luke 24:47; Acts 10:43). Rome requires confession to a priest for mortal sin [CCC 1456, 1497]. No apostle ever hears a private confession and absolves.
defense.askBack: *"When Peter preached in Acts 10, how did Cornelius get forgiven?"*

defense.objection: "2 Thess 2:15: hold to traditions, spoken *or* written."
defense.response: The tradition Paul means is the gospel he preached in person (2:14). It was spoken *or* written; it wasn't a second, different body of teaching. Name one doctrine handed down orally that we can verify came from Paul.
defense.askBack: *"Which of Paul's oral traditions can you name that isn't in Scripture?"*

defense.objection: "1 Tim 3:15: the church is the pillar and support of the truth."
defense.response: The context is a local church's conduct, with elders and deacons (3:1–14). A pillar *holds up* the truth; it doesn't *create* it. The truth it holds up is Christ (3:16).
defense.askBack: *"Does a pillar make the roof, or hold it up?"*

defense.objection: "Matt 16:18: Peter is the rock and the first pope."
defense.response: Rome teaches this [CCC 881–882]. But Peter calls *Christ* the stone (1 Pet 2:4–8), and Paul says no foundation can be laid except Christ (1 Cor 3:11). The keys and binding go to all the disciples (Matt 18:18). Nothing in the text says anything about successors or Rome.
defense.askBack: *"Where does the passage mention a successor?"*

defense.objection: "The pope is infallible when he speaks ex cathedra."
defense.response: Vatican I defined it [Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4]. Yet Peter himself was publicly rebuked for compromising the gospel (Gal 2:11–14). At the Jerusalem council, James gave the judgment (Acts 15:13–21). Peter called himself a "fellow elder" (1 Pet 5:1).
defense.askBack: *"If Peter could be wrong on the gospel, can his successor?"*

defense.objection: "Mary was conceived without sin (Immaculate Conception)."
defense.response: Defined in 1854 [CCC 491]. Mary calls God "my Savior" (Luke 1:47). She offered the sin offering after childbirth (Luke 2:22–24; Lev 12:6–8), and Scripture says all have sinned. No text exempts her.
defense.askBack: *"Why would a sinless woman need a Savior and a sin offering?"*

defense.objection: "Mary was ever-virgin."
defense.response: Rome teaches it [CCC 499–500, 510]. Joseph "kept her a virgin until she gave birth" (Matt 1:25). The Gospels name Jesus' brothers and mention sisters, with His mother (Matt 13:55–56; Mark 6:3; Acts 1:14). Rome reads these as relatives [CCC 500]. The plain sense is siblings.
defense.askBack: *"If 'brothers' with 'His mother' means cousins here, how would Mark have said brothers?"*

defense.objection: "Mary was assumed body and soul into heaven."
defense.response: It was defined as dogma in 1950 [Munificentissimus Deus 44]. Scripture says nothing about it. Binding a doctrine with no biblical witness is the very authority question again.
defense.askBack: *"What verse would you give a new believer for this?"*

defense.objection: "Purgatory: 1 Cor 3:15, 'saved, yet so as through fire.'"
defense.response: That passage is about testing a minister's *work* (3:10–14), not purging a person's sins. To be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Cor 5:8). The thief went to paradise *today* (Luke 23:43). Rome also cites 2 Macc 12:43–45 [CCC 1032], which isn't Scripture (see below).
defense.askBack: *"In 1 Cor 3, what gets burned: the man's sins or his work?"*

defense.objection: "Indulgences can reduce temporal punishment, even for the dead."
defense.response: Rome teaches this [CCC 1471, 1479, 1498]. Christ "made purification of sins" (Heb 1:3), and the gift of God isn't obtained by works or payments (Acts 8:20; Isa 55:1). Indulgences assume a debt that Christ left unpaid. Rome says they draw on a "treasury" that includes the prayers and good works of Mary and the saints [CCC 1476–1477]. Scripture knows no one with righteousness to spare: when we have done everything, we are still unworthy slaves (Luke 17:10).
defense.askBack: *"Did Christ pay all of it, or only part?"*

defense.objection: "Baptism regenerates (John 3:5; Acts 2:38; 1 Pet 3:21)."
defense.response: Rome teaches justification is conferred in baptism [CCC 1992, 1213, 1263]. But Cornelius received the Spirit *before* baptism (Acts 10:44–48), and the thief was saved without it. Peter says it is "not the removal of dirt… but an appeal to God" (1 Pet 3:21). Spurgeon: "Baptism without faith saves no one".
defense.askBack: *"If baptism saves, why does Paul say Christ didn't send him to baptize?"*

defense.objection: "You removed seven books (the Apocrypha)."
defense.response: Trent declared them canonical [Sess. 4]. The OT was entrusted to the Jews (Rom 3:2), and they never received these books. Jesus framed Scripture as Law, Prophets and Psalms (Luke 24:44). The NT never quotes them as Scripture.
defense.askBack: *"Did Israel ever receive 2 Maccabees as Scripture?"*

defense.objection: "Sola Scriptura isn't in the Bible."
defense.response: Scripture is the only revelation called God-breathed (2 Tim 3:16). Jesus judged tradition by it (Mark 7:13), and Isaiah sends us "to the law and to the testimony" (Isa 8:20). Busenitz traces this conviction through the fathers: Athanasius said "the sacred and inspired Scriptures are sufficient".
defense.askBack: *"What else does Scripture call God-breathed?"*

defense.objection: "We need priests and sacraments; grace flows through the Church."
defense.response: Rome holds that the sacraments are necessary for salvation [CCC 1129]. Christ holds His priesthood permanently (Heb 7:23–25), the veil is torn (Matt 27:51), and every believer is a priest (1 Pet 2:9).
defense.askBack: *"Who does Hebrews say we can approach God through?"*

defense.objection: "Catholics and evangelicals believe the same gospel now."
defense.response: Trent's canons on justification have never been revoked, and they are quoted in the current Catechism (CCC 1992 echoes Trent). MacArthur: "nothing has changed since Trent". Being kind doesn't mean treating the difference as minor.
defense.askBack: *"Has Rome withdrawn Trent's anathema on faith alone?"*

defense.objection: "Mary is the Mother of God."
defense.response: Rome teaches this [CCC 495]. The One she bore is truly God (Luke 1:35, 43), but she is mother to His humanity. His deity has no mother and no beginning (John 1:1; Mic 5:2). Scripture's own name for her is "the mother of Jesus." The title is used to lift her up; Mary used her own words to lift Him up.
defense.askBack: *"What does Mary call God in Luke 1:47?"*

defense.objection: "Mary is the Queen of Heaven."
defense.response: Rome says she was exalted "as Queen over all things" [CCC 966]. Scripture uses "queen of heaven" only for a false goddess whose worship God judged (Jer 7:18; 44:17–19, 25). A Catholic will say that is a different figure, and it is. The point is that Scripture never gives Mary a throne. She calls herself the Lord's slave, and in heaven every creature worships God and the Lamb.
defense.askBack: *"In Revelation 4 and 5, who is on the throne, and who is worshiped?"*

defense.objection: "Mary cooperated in our redemption, and graces come to us through her."
defense.response: MacArthur calls Co-Redemptrix "unofficial reality" in Rome even though it was never made dogma, and he calls the idea blasphemous. In 2025 the Vatican's doctrine office said the *title* is not appropriate [Mater Populi Fidelis]. The teaching did not change. The Catechism still says she cooperated "in the Savior's work" and still calls her Advocate, Helper, Benefactress and Mediatrix [CCC 968–969], and John Paul II used the title Co-Redemptrix himself. If they say "the Church dropped that," ask which paragraph of the Catechism was removed. None was. (The word "Co-Redemptrix" is not in the Catechism, so quote 968–969, not the title.) Scripture: there is no savior besides God, and our High Priest is not hard to reach.
defense.askBack: *"If the title is wrong, why does the Catechism still call her Mediatrix?"*

defense.objection: "Mary has appeared: Guadalupe, Lourdes, Fatima."
defense.response: Rome itself says no one is bound to believe private revelations [CCC 67]. Scripture tells us to test every spirit. A sign or vision that turns prayer and trust toward anyone but God fails the test, whoever seems to bring it. Mary is never seen again in Scripture after Acts 1:14.
defense.askBack: *"If even an angel from heaven can't change the gospel, can an apparition?"*

defense.objection: "The rosary: 'pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death.'"
defense.response: The Hail Mary entrusts the hour of death to her care [CCC 2677], and the five decades have 53 Hail Marys to 6 Our Fathers. In Scripture the dying man calls on the Lord, and He hears. Jesus told us to pray to the Father, to ask in His own name, and not to pile up repeated words.
defense.askBack: *"In Psalm 116, who does the dying man call on?"*

defense.objection: "Statues and images only remind us of the person, like a family photo."
defense.response: Rome teaches that honor given to an image passes to the one it shows [CCC 2132]. The commandment forbids the bowing, not only the making. The Psalms say those who trust in images become like them, and Isaiah speaks of those who "pray to a god who cannot save." See [the icons play](/orthodox/case/play-3).
defense.askBack: *"Does the commandment forbid only making images, or also bowing to them?"*

defense.objection: "We adore Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament."
defense.response: Rome teaches the consecrated host is to be given the worship due to God [CCC 1378; Trent, Sess. 13, can. 6]. If the bread is still bread, that is worship given to a created thing. Christ's body is in heaven, where He sat down and waits until He returns. This was the point the English martyrs died for.
defense.askBack: *"According to Acts 3:21, where is Christ's body now?"*

defense.objection: "The pope is the Vicar of Christ and head of the Church."
defense.response: Rome teaches this [CCC 882]. Scripture gives the headship to Christ alone. The One Jesus sent to stand in His place is the Holy Spirit. "Holy Father" is what Jesus calls the Father. Peter calls himself a fellow elder and tells elders not to lord it over the flock.
defense.askBack: *"In John 17:11, who does Jesus call 'Holy Father'?"*

defense.objection: "Peter was the first bishop of Rome, and the popes succeed him."
defense.response: Scripture never shows it. Paul writes to Rome and greets two dozen people with no mention of Peter, and says he does not build on another man's foundation. Peter was sent to the circumcised. This is an argument from silence, so say so. But even if Peter died in Rome, no text passes his office on. "Strengthen your brothers" and "Tend My sheep" restore a man who had denied Him, and Peter gives the same charge to every elder. The earliest writings connected with Rome (1 Clement, Ignatius's letter to the Romans, the Shepherd of Hermas) speak of elders who lead the church and name no single ruling bishop there. Augustine took the rock of Matt 16:18 to be Christ, whom Peter confessed.
defense.askBack: *"Why doesn't Paul greet Peter in Romans 16?"*

defense.objection: "Priests must be celibate."
defense.response: Rome treats this as a discipline, not a doctrine: its Eastern-rite priests may be married [CCC 1579–1580]. Scripture's overseers are normally married men, Peter had a wife, and Paul warns about those who forbid marriage. Singleness is a gift to some, not a rule for an office.
defense.askBack: *"In 1 Timothy 3:2, what does Paul expect of an overseer?"*

defense.objection: "We're saved through faith, baptism and keeping the commandments."
defense.response: That is Rome's own wording: salvation "through faith, Baptism and the observance of the Commandments" [CCC 2068, quoting Vatican II]. If they say the works are done by grace [CCC 2008], it changes nothing: grace plus works is still not grace (Rom 11:6). In Acts 15 some said faith was not enough without circumcision and the Law of Moses. Peter answered that God cleanses hearts by faith and that we are saved "through the grace of the Lord Jesus." Paul says that if you add a requirement to be justified, Christ will be of no benefit to you.
defense.askBack: *"At the Jerusalem council, which side did Peter take?"*

defense.objection: "We believe in grace, faith and Scripture too."
defense.response: Rome uses all three words. It says each one is *necessary*. The disagreement is whether each one is *enough*. Is Scripture enough to equip the man of God, or must tradition be added? Is faith enough to justify, or must works be added? Is Christ's one offering enough, or must it be offered again?
defense.askBack: *"Necessary, or enough? Which word would you use for what Christ did?"*

defense.objection: "The Church has taught the same faith for 2,000 years."
defense.response: Compare two of Rome's own documents. In 1302 Pope Boniface VIII defined that it is "absolutely necessary for salvation" for every human being to be subject to the Roman Pontiff [Unam Sanctam]. Today's Catechism says the plan of salvation includes Muslims, and that people who do not know the gospel through no fault of their own can be saved [CCC 841, 847]. Rome's answer is that doctrine "develops." That is Cardinal Newman's argument from 1845, and it admits that the teaching has not stayed the same. Scripture speaks of a faith delivered once for all.
defense.askBack: *"If both statements are official teaching, which one do I follow?"*

defense.objection: "It's the same Jesus. Does the rest really matter?" / "Are you saying Catholics aren't Christians?"
defense.response: Say it plainly and with love: Rome teaches a different gospel. Paul's opponents in Galatia believed in Jesus, His cross and His resurrection, and added one requirement. He called it a different gospel, put it under God's curse, said those who receive it are "severed from Christ," and warned that a little leaven leavens the whole lump. MacArthur: Roman Catholicism is "false Christianity teaching a false gospel," and "people need to be rescued from this system." Busenitz: unless Rome's false doctrines are rejected, there is no hope of salvation in that system. A person is saved only by turning from every other trust to Christ alone, and a person who has done that cannot stay at peace with what Rome teaches.
defense.askBack: *"I'm not asking which church you belong to. What are you trusting to make you right with God?"*

defense.objection: "My family would never forgive me if I left."
defense.response: Take this seriously; it is often the real obstacle. In Jesus' day people believed and stayed silent because confessing Him meant being put out of the synagogue. He never hid the cost, and He promised that no one who leaves family for His sake will lose by it. You may not need to tell them to leave anything today. Ask them to settle first who they are trusting.
defense.askBack: *"If it were true, would you want to know, even if it cost you?"*

items.text: "I was born Catholic and I'll die Catholic." (Don't argue identity. Say *"I'm not asking you to change teams; I'm asking what you're trusting."* Leave them Rom 4:5 and 1 John 5:13.)
"I'll ask my priest." (Good. Write down two questions for him: *"Can I know I have eternal life (1 John 5:13)?"* and *"What does Heb 10:18 mean?"* Then follow up.)
"You're just interpreting it your way." (Agree that everyone interprets. Then read the passage out loud together and ask *"What does it say?"* before *"What does it mean?"*)

beliefs.text: Revelation is preserved "by two channels: holy tradition and holy Scripture," and the Church is "the sure repository of holy tradition" [Philaret, *Longer Catechism*, Q16, Q18]. Scripture is to be believed "not otherwise than as the Catholic Church has interpreted," and the Church "cannot err" [Confession of Dositheus, Decrees 2, 12]. Salvation is theosis, "to share in the life of God," and grace and human effort work together (synergy) [GOARCH, "Spirituality"; Philaret Q3–5]. A man is justified "not… through faith alone, but through faith which works through love, that is to say, through faith and works" [Dositheus, Decree 13]. The OCA's current adult manual adds: "Justification therefore is not a single, once-for-all event" [OCA, *Essential Orthodox Christian Beliefs* (2023), p. 218]. Icons receive veneration, "not the full adoration (*latria*)… paid only to the divine nature" [Nicaea II, Definition]. Orthodoxy has no single catechism. Above, conciliar sources (Nicaea II, Dositheus) carry more weight than catechisms and manuals (Philaret, OCA), and you should say which one you're quoting.

lead.label: Where we agree
lead.text: They hold firmly to the Nicene Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Christ (Chalcedon), the virgin birth, the bodily resurrection, Christ's return, and eternal judgment. They reject the papacy and the Immaculate Conception, and generally reject purgatory as Rome defines it, though they pray for the departed [Dositheus, Decree 18]. Their liturgy is full of Scripture. And justification was never the fight in the East that it was with Rome, so some Orthodox writers sound close to us on it. Say this out loud.

lead.label: Approach
lead.text: Most American Orthodox you'll meet are either cradle Orthodox (it's family and ethnicity) or converts, often young men drawn by beauty, history and seriousness. With converts, don't attack the liturgy. Ask what *authority* tests it. White's warning: Orthodoxy "is an enigma, not only to most in the West, but to itself," and "is not merely Romanism without a Pope". So don't assume Catholic answers fit. Use their own sources (Philaret Q23 is your best friend), keep pressing Scripture as the test, and land on the gospel every time.

cheatCard.text: **2 Tim 3:16–17**: *"If Scripture equips the man of God for every good work, what's still missing?"*
**Mark 7:8–13**: *"Can a tradition that's very old still cancel God's word?"*
**Ex 20:4–5**: *"Does the command forbid only making images, or also bowing to them?"*
**Isa 53:5–6, 10**: *"Who laid our iniquity on the Servant, and who was pleased to crush Him?"*
**Rom 5:1**: *"'Having been justified': is that finished or still in progress?"*
**Eph 2:1–5**: *"Before God made us alive, were we sick or dead?"*

altOpeners.text: *"If an old tradition and a clear verse disagreed, which would win?"*

chain.text: **Philaret Q23** (not Scripture, but theirs): tradition must agree with Scripture. *"So Scripture is the test of tradition?"*
**Mark 7:8–13**: Jesus judged a long, respected tradition by Scripture and found it "invalidating the word of God." *"Was age a defense?"*
**Acts 17:11**: The Bereans tested even Paul by the Scriptures. *"Is anyone above that test?"*
**2 Tim 3:15–17**: Scripture makes "wise for salvation" and "fully equipped." *"So it can do the testing?"*
**Gal 1:8–9**: Even an angel's gospel is tested by the apostolic one. *"Then let's test how we're saved by Scripture. Agreed?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Only the Church can interpret Scripture [Dositheus, Decree 2]."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Then Philaret's test can never fail, because the Church grades its own test. Cyril of Jerusalem (an Eastern father) told his hearers not to believe even him "unless you receive the proof… from the divine Scriptures," and Basil said hearers should examine teachers, "receiving what is in conformity with the Scriptures and rejecting what is opposed to them".

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Basil said unwritten tradition has the same force [quoted in Philaret Q24]."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Basil said both. Ask: *"Which of the two lets you correct an error if one creeps in?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"1 Tim 3:15: the Church is the pillar of truth."*
ifTheySay.youSay: See the defense table.

opener.text: *"Would you agree that we must only follow tradition that agrees with Scripture?"* (Their own catechism says so: "We must follow that tradition which agrees with the divine revelation and with holy Scripture" [Philaret Q23].)

closer.text: *"If Scripture tests tradition, let it test the biggest question: how is a sinner made right with God? Romans says by faith in Christ, apart from works (Rom 3:28; 4:5), with repentance (Acts 20:21). Will you read Romans 3–5 with me?"*

offense.title: Justified now
offense.subtitle: against salvation as a lifelong process

altOpeners.text: *"Your church's manual says justification 'is not a single, once-for-all event' [OCA EOCB, p. 218]. Can we look at what Paul says?"*

chain.text: **Luke 18:13–14**: The tax collector cried for mercy and "went down to his house justified." (The OCA manual cites this verse too [EOCB p. 218].) *"Was he justified on the way home, or still in process?"*
**Rom 4:4–5**: Credited to "the one who does not work, but believes." *"Where is synergy in that sentence?"*
**Rom 5:1**: "Having been justified by faith, we have peace." *"Past or future?"*
**Rom 8:1, 33–34**: "No condemnation." "God is the one who justifies; who is the one who condemns?" *"Is that a courtroom verdict?"*
**Heb 10:14**: "Perfected for all time." *"How long is 'for all time'?"*
**Eph 2:8–10**: Saved by grace through faith, not of works, *for* good works. *"Where do works go: before or after?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Faith working through love (Gal 5:6), so faith and works [Dositheus 13]."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Gal 5:6 describes what living faith *does*. The same letter says we're justified "by faith in Christ and not by the works of the Law" (Gal 2:16), and condemns adding anything (Gal 3:1–3).

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Salvation is healing and union, not a legal transaction."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Scripture uses both: a verdict (Rom 8:33–34) *and* new life (2 Cor 5:17). We agree on union and transformation (2 Cor 3:18). We don't let healing replace the verdict.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Faith alone is easy believism."*
ifTheySay.youSay: No. Saving faith repents and submits to Christ as Lord (Luke 13:3; Rom 10:9). Works are fruit, not a co-cause.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Isn't that the Protestant reading? The fathers taught synergy."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Busenitz collects patristic witnesses to justification by faith, e.g., Clement of Rome: "not justified by ourselves… but by that faith". Letham notes some honored Orthodox writers who sound the same note.

opener.text: *"Can a person be declared righteous by God today, completely, and know it?"*

closer.text: *"The tax collector didn't bring a process, just a plea, and went home justified. Will you stop leaning on your progress and trust Christ's finished work today (Luke 18:13–14; Rom 4:5)?"*

altOpeners.text: *"When Israel made the golden calf, who did Aaron say they were worshiping?"* (Ex 32:4–5: a "feast to Yahweh.")

chain.text: **Ex 20:4–5**: Not just making; "you shall not worship them or serve them." *"Is the act of bowing itself in view?"*
**Deut 4:15–19**: "You did not see any form on the day Yahweh spoke," so don't make one. *"Why does Moses ground it in what they *didn't* see?"*
**Ex 32:4–5**: The calf was meant to honor Yahweh, and God still judged it. *"Does good intention make a bowed-to image acceptable?"*

**2 Kings 18:4**: Hezekiah smashed the bronze serpent, an object *God commanded* (Num 21:8–9), because Israel burned incense to it. *"If a God-commanded image became an idol when venerated, what about one God never commanded?"*
**John 4:23–24**: The Father seeks those who worship "in spirit and truth." **Col 1:15**: Christ *is* the image of the invisible God. *"Do we need another image to reach the true Image?"*
**1 John 5:21**: "Guard yourselves from idols," written to Christians after the Incarnation.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"We give icons veneration, not worship (latria); the honor passes to the prototype [Nicaea II; CCC 2132 says the same]."*
ifTheySay.youSay: That is their position. The commandment forbids the bowing, not just a wrong inner attitude. Schooping, a former Orthodox priest, asks how mere "veneration" of an image becomes worship of Christ: if it doesn't, it's too little for Christ; if it does, it's worship given through an image.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"God commanded cherubim in the tabernacle (Ex 25:18)."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Yes, images can exist. But no one was ever told to bow to, kiss or pray before them, and the bronze serpent shows what happens when they do (2 Kings 18:4).

ifTheySay.theySay: *"The Incarnation made God visible, so we can picture Him."*
ifTheySay.youSay: God made Himself visible *in Christ* (John 14:9). Ortlund documents that early Christians did not bow to images, and that icon veneration came later; he notes that Epiphanius opposed it in the 4th century.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Nicaea II anathematizes people who refuse to venerate icons."*
ifTheySay.youSay: It does: "If anyone does not salute such representations… let him be anathema" [Nicaea II, anathemas]. Ask gently: *"Was every Christian before 787 who didn't kiss icons under a curse?"*

opener.text: *"Does the second commandment forbid only making images, or also bowing down to them?"* (Ex 20:5)

closer.text: *"Christ is the Image of God, and He invites you to come to Him directly, by faith, with no object in between (Heb 4:16; 10:19–22). Will you?"*

altOpeners.text: *"Was Jesus punished in our place, or only defeating death for us?"*

chain.text: **Isa 53:5–6**: "Pierced through for *our* transgressions… Yahweh has caused the iniquity of us all to fall on Him." *"Is that substitution?"*
**Isa 53:10**: "Yahweh was pleased to crush Him… a guilt offering." *"Who is acting in this verse?"*
**Gal 3:13**: Christ redeemed us from the curse "having become a curse for us." *"Whose curse did He bear?"*
**2 Cor 5:21; 1 Pet 2:24; 3:18**: Made sin for us; bore our sins in His body; "the just for the unjust." *"In whose place?"*
**Rom 3:25–26**: A propitiation, so that God is "just and the justifier." *"Why does God's justice need to be shown at the cross?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"That makes the Father a vengeful pagan god punishing a 'whipping boy' [OCA EOCB, pp. 186–88]."*
ifTheySay.youSay: We reject that caricature too. Father and Son act together in love (John 10:17–18; Rom 8:32; 1 John 4:10). The OCA manual itself affirms that justification "stands alongside others" as a biblical metaphor [EOCB p. 188]. This isn't a conciliar dogma for them, so ask what *this* person believes.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"It's Anselm's medieval theory."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Isaiah 53 is seven centuries before Christ. Schooping, a former Orthodox priest, shows a substitutionary reading in Chrysostom and Theophylact.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"The East teaches Christus Victor."*
ifTheySay.youSay: So does Scripture (Col 2:15; Heb 2:14–15). But Col 2:14 says the victory came by canceling "the certificate of debt" against us. Both are true together.

opener.text: *"In Isaiah 53, whose iniquity did Yahweh lay on the Servant?"*

closer.text: *"He bore the penalty in your place, and He offers you His righteousness as a gift (2 Cor 5:21). Will you turn from your sin and receive it by faith?"*

altOpeners.text: *"Do you believe we inherit only death from Adam, or also guilt?"* (The OCA says "only Adam and Eve are guilty of that sin" [OCA Q&A, "Original Sin"].)

chain.text: **Eph 2:1–3**: "Dead in your trespasses… by nature children of wrath." *"Does a neutral nature deserve wrath?"*

**Rom 5:12, 18–19**: "Through one transgression there resulted condemnation to all men… through the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners." *"Condemnation is a guilty verdict, not only a sickness, right?"*
**Ps 51:5**: "In sin my mother conceived me." *"When does David trace his sin back to?"*
**John 3:3–7**: "You must be born again." *"Can the dead cooperate in their own birth?"*
**Eph 2:4–9**: "But God… made us alive… by grace you have been saved… not of works." *"Who did the raising?"*

ifTheySay.theySay: *"That's Augustine. The East never accepted original guilt."*
ifTheySay.youSay: Paul wrote Rom 5 centuries before Augustine. Also note that the Confession of Dositheus says infants "are subject to original sin" and need its remission [Decree 16], so Orthodox sources themselves aren't unanimous.

ifTheySay.theySay: *"Then infants who die go to hell?"*
ifTheySay.youSay: Our hope rests in God's mercy and character (2 Sam 12:23). It doesn't rest on denying what Rom 5 says about Adam.

opener.text: *"Before God made us alive, how does Paul describe us: sick or dead?"* (Eph 2:1)

closer.text: *"Dead people don't need coaching. They need resurrection, and only Christ gives it, by grace through faith (Eph 2:4–9). Will you ask Him for that life?"*

defense.objection: "Sola Scriptura is a 16th-century invention."
defense.response: The fathers treated Scripture as the final court, including *Eastern* fathers. Athanasius: "the sacred and inspired Scriptures are sufficient to declare the truth." Cyril of Jerusalem: don't believe even me without proof from Scripture.
defense.askBack: *"Were Athanasius and Cyril Protestants?"*

defense.objection: "The Church is the pillar and ground of the truth (1 Tim 3:15)."
defense.response: Philaret uses this verse [Q18]. The context is a local congregation with elders and deacons. A pillar holds up the truth; it doesn't author it.
defense.askBack: *"Does a pillar make the truth or hold it up?"*

defense.objection: "Hold the traditions, by word or letter (2 Thess 2:15)."
defense.response: Philaret quotes this verse *to say tradition must agree with Scripture* [Q23]. Paul's tradition is the gospel (2:14), not a separate source.
defense.askBack: *"Your catechism says tradition must agree with Scripture. So which one tests the other?"*

defense.objection: "We are the one true Church; you split off."
defense.response: The Church is all who are united to Christ by faith (Eph 2:19–22). Our church holds that each local church is self-governing under Christ. Schooping, from the inside, calls Orthodox ecclesiology "inextricably exclusive".
defense.askBack: *"Is someone who trusts Christ alone, outside your communion, in Christ?"*

defense.objection: "We have apostolic succession from the apostles."
defense.response: Apostles had to be eyewitnesses of the risen Christ (Acts 1:21–22); the foundation was laid once (Eph 2:20). The succession Paul commands is of *teaching* (2 Tim 2:2). He warned that men in the succession would rise up teaching error (Acts 20:29–30).
defense.askBack: *"Can a bishop in succession teach error?"*

defense.objection: "Theosis: 'God became man so man might become god.'"
defense.response: Ask what they mean first. They do *not* mean sharing God's essence (they distinguish essence and energies). We agree on union with Christ and glorification (Rom 8:29–30; 1 John 3:2). We differ on making it a cooperative process that grounds acceptance with God.
defense.askBack: *"Is theosis the ground of your acceptance with God, or the fruit of it?"*

defense.objection: "Salvation is synergy: God and I working together."
defense.response: Philaret: a right faith "and good works" are necessary "to save one's own soul" [Q3]. Scripture says God gives the faith and raises the dead (Eph 2:5, 8–9; John 6:44). We work *out* what He has worked *in* (Phil 2:12–13).
defense.askBack: *"In Phil 2:13, who is doing the working?"*

defense.objection: "Icons have always been part of the Church."
defense.response: Ortlund documents that early Christians did not bow to or kiss images, and that 4th-century voices like Epiphanius opposed it. Veneration was defined in 787 [Nicaea II].
defense.askBack: *"Can you show icon veneration in the New Testament?"*

defense.objection: "Mary is the Theotokos."
defense.response: The title means "God-bearer," and it was first used to guard a truth we hold: the One she bore is truly God (Luke 1:35, 43). But she is mother to His humanity. His deity has no mother and no beginning (John 1:1; Mic 5:2). Scripture's own name for her is "the mother of Jesus" (Acts 1:14). We part ways where the title is used to lift her up, pray to her, or call her ever-virgin.
defense.askBack: *"Do you mean she bore the One who is God, or that she shares in His glory?"*

defense.objection: "Mary is ever-virgin."
defense.response: Philaret teaches it [Q186]. Matt 1:25 says "until she gave birth," and the Gospels name His brothers alongside His mother (Matt 13:55–56; Mark 6:3). Orthodox usually explain these as Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. The plain sense is siblings.
defense.askBack: *"What would Mark write if he meant siblings?"*

defense.objection: "Asking the saints to pray is like asking a friend."
defense.response: The OCA manual says this, and adds that the saints help and heal "themselves" too [EOCB p. 72]. Scripture models asking the living (James 5:16), never the departed, and gives us direct access through Christ (Heb 4:16; 7:25). Busenitz notes how such practices developed historically, citing Calvin's *Treatise on Relics*.
defense.askBack: *"Who does Hebrews tell you to approach for help in time of need?"*

defense.objection: "Baptism saves (John 3:5; 1 Pet 3:21)."
defense.response: Dositheus: without baptism "none is able to be saved" [Decree 16]. But the Spirit came on Cornelius before baptism (Acts 10:44–48), and Peter says baptism saves "not [as] the removal of dirt… but an appeal to God." Spurgeon: "Baptism without faith saves no one."
defense.askBack: *"Was the thief on the cross saved?"*

defense.objection: "The Eucharist is truly His body and blood."
defense.response: Dositheus affirms a change of substance [Decree 17]. Our church holds that the elements represent Christ's body and blood, *and* that the Supper is a real communion with the risen Christ (1 Cor 10:16). Jesus' words are spirit (John 6:63), and His sacrifice is not repeated (Heb 10:14, 18).
defense.askBack: *"Does the Supper proclaim His death, or offer it again?"*

defense.objection: "God isn't angry. Sin is sickness, not crime."
defense.response: Sin is both disease and guilt. Scripture speaks of wrath (Rom 1:18; John 3:36) and of a verdict (Rom 5:18). The OCA manual itself keeps "justification (our acquittal)" as a biblical theme [EOCB p. 188].
defense.askBack: *"Does John 3:36 say the wrath 'abides' or 'heals'?"*

defense.objection: "We don't inherit guilt, only death."
defense.response: The OCA says so [Q&A, "Original Sin"]. Rom 5:18–19 says one man's disobedience brought "condemnation to all men" and "made" many sinners. Dositheus speaks of infants' "original sin" [Decree 16].
defense.askBack: *"What does 'condemnation to all men' mean?"*

defense.objection: "Our church is 2,000 years old; yours is 500."
defense.response: The test is whether a church holds the apostles' teaching (Acts 2:42; Gal 1:8). Age doesn't settle it: the Pharisees' traditions were old too (Mark 7:13). Busenitz shows Scripture-alone convictions in the early church.
defense.askBack: *"If a 2,000-year-old church taught error, how would anyone know?"*

defense.objection: "The Divine Liturgy is ancient and beautiful. Protestant worship is shallow."
defense.response: Shallow worship anywhere is a fault, but age and beauty do not make worship true. Justin Martyr (c. 150) describes the early service as reading the apostles and prophets, preaching, prayer, and the Supper. Letham's concern is that Orthodoxy downplays preaching. Tozer: God tired of rituals that pointed ahead; Christ fulfilled them.
defense.askBack: *"What did the earliest services you can document center on?"*

defense.objection: "Toll houses / the soul's journey after death."
defense.response: Toll houses are not dogma, even in ROCOR, which declined to define them in 1980. Don't argue it as if it were their official teaching. Scripture: to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Cor 5:8; Luke 23:43).
defense.askBack: *"Is that a teaching you're bound to, or a pious opinion?"*

defense.objection: "God is known in His energies, not His essence. Theology is experience, not propositions."
defense.response: Keep it short. God truly reveals Himself in His word, and we can know Him truly, though not exhaustively (John 17:3; 1 Tim 6:16). Letham's concern is that Palamas's framework can lead to agnosticism about God. Then bring it back to the gospel.
defense.askBack: *"Can God tell us true things about Himself in words?"*

defense.objection: "We pray for the departed, and our prayers help them."
defense.response: The Confession of Dositheus says that some who repented without bearing fruit go to Hades and are delivered by "the prayers of the priests" and the good works of their relatives [Decree 18]. They will say it is not purgatory. It is still a second chance after death, and Scripture gives none. Scripture teaches that death is followed by judgment, that a great chasm is fixed, and that the believer who leaves the body is at home with the Lord. It never shows a prayer changing anyone's state after death.
defense.askBack: *"If today is the day of salvation, what are we telling people who plan to be prayed out later?"*

defense.objection: "Our infants are baptized, chrismated and given communion."
defense.response: That is their practice: baptized and chrismated infants receive communion [OCA, *The Orthodox Faith*, vol. 2]. It follows from believing that baptism gives new birth (see the baptism row). In Scripture those who "received his word" were baptized and then shared in the breaking of bread, and each person is told to examine himself before he eats. Our church baptizes believers, by immersion, and the Supper is for those who profess faith.
defense.askBack: *"Can an infant examine himself?"*

defense.objection: "I'd lose my family and my people if I left the Church."
defense.response: For many cradle Orthodox, church, family and nation are one thing, so this is the real obstacle. Don't wave it away. Jesus never hid the cost and promised that no one who leaves family for His sake will lose by it. Ask them to settle first who they are trusting.
defense.askBack: *"If it were true, would you want to know, even if it cost you?"*

items.text: "You have to experience the Liturgy to understand." (Accept the invitation kindly if you want to, then ask them to come read Romans 3–5 with you. Experience vs. Scripture is the whole question.)
"You're reading the Bible outside the Church." (Say: *"Then let's read it with Cyril and Athanasius,"* and quote their Scripture-first lines.)
